An empirical study of existing open-source projects · CMPT 479 · Simon Xie, Sukhdip Kandola, Thang To

Is TypeScript written by AI coding agents better or worse than code written by people?

We ran the same automatic quality checks on — real open-source projects. The short answer: the AI-built code is much tidier, with about —× fewer lint problems, but its functions are more tangled. On testing, there are too few projects to tell the groups apart.

Written by people— projects, each frozen at its last commit before 2021, before AI coding assistants existed, so no AI could have written them.

Built by AI coding agents— projects created in 2025 or later where most commits are signed by an agent such as Claude Code, Cursor or Codex.

How the comparison works

Pick fair pairs

GitHub search found — candidates; — passed screening. We kept — AI projects, each paired with a human one of similar size.

Freeze the code

Every project is checked at one fixed commit, so anyone can repeat the measurement and get the same result.

Run identical checks

The same seven automatic checks in the same Docker container: lint rules, copy-paste, install, compile, run the tests, and plant bugs to see if the tests catch them.

Ask: real or chance?

We compare the typical (median) project of each group and test whether a gap is too large to be luck with this few projects per side.

What we found

Finding 1 · code quality

AI-built code breaks far fewer lint rules

Lint problems per 1,000 lines in the typical project. A lint problem is a rule broken in the code: an unused variable, a risky comparison, a let that should be const.

Caveat: some of today's rules didn't exist when the human code was written. Counting only rules from before 2021, the gap shrinks to — vs —, and that could be chance.

How to read: each dot is one project. The tall line is the typical project of each group. Further left is better.

Finding 2 · type safety

AI agents almost never switch off TypeScript's type checking

—People
—AI agents

Uses of the type any per 1,000 lines. Writing any tells the compiler "don't check this value", which hides the mistakes TypeScript exists to catch.

—

How to read: each dot is one project; most AI projects sit at zero. Further left is better.

Finding 3 · complexity

But AI-written functions are more tangled

—People
—AI agents

Average number of paths through a function (each if, loop or && adds one). More paths means more cases to understand and to test. Functions too branchy to test easily (more than 10 paths): —% for people, —% for AI agents.

How to read: each dot is one project. Here the AI dots sit to the right, the worse side.

Finding 4 · does it still work?

More AI projects still compile and pass their tests

— of —People: tests pass
— of —AI agents: tests pass

The human code is years old. For — of the — human projects that no longer compile, the errors are in libraries it downloads or the install itself fails. Re-running the failing human tests on the Node.js version of their time rescued only — of —.

Caveat: with this few projects per group, a gap of a few projects is a tendency, not proof.

How to read: one square per project. Filled means the check passed; an empty outline means it failed. Hover a square for the project.

Finding 5 · test strength

Do their tests catch bugs? Too few projects to tell

—AI agents, — projects

Share of deliberately planted bugs (a < turned into <=, a true into false) that make at least one test fail. This only works on projects whose tests pass, which leaves very few human projects.

Every measure at a glance

Which group comes out better on each measure, and how clearly

How to read: a bar pointing right means AI agents did better; pointing left means people did. The longer the bar, the more consistently one group beat the other (full length means every project of one group beat every project of the other). Solid bars are clear differences; faded bars could be chance. Hover a bar for the typical values.

Left out: functions per 1,000 lines, where neither direction is better.

Can you trust the numbers? We re-ran one project live

Project L01 (built by an AI agent) went through the whole pipeline again on Nov 7 in a fresh container. It took — seconds, and — of — measurements came out exactly the same as the stored results.

Definitions and method details
Typical project
The median: half the projects in the group score higher, half lower. Used instead of the average so one extreme project can't skew the result.
Lint problems
ESLint 9 with typescript-eslint and SonarJS rules, the same configuration for every project, ignoring the project's own settings and any "disable" comments.
Paths per function
Cyclomatic complexity (McCabe): the number of independent paths through a function. Above 10 is commonly treated as hard to test.
Planted bugs caught
Mutation score from StrykerJS 10: killed mutants over all valid mutants, on a seeded sample of about 400 lines per project.
Clear difference
Mann–Whitney U test, corrected for testing all the measures at once (Holm). "Clear" means the corrected p-value is below 0.05: a gap this large would rarely appear by luck.
Bar length
Cliff's δ: the chance a random project from one group beats a random project from the other, minus the reverse. Above 0.47 counts as a large effect.
Left out
H06 from mutation testing (its tests run compiled output), and mutation runs where more than half the planted bugs timed out.
